title: Habakkuk: by faithfulness (Habakkuk 2:4)
hookLine: the Talmud says Habakkuk reduced the whole Torah to one line: the righteous live by faith (Makkot 24a)

cards: "O LORD, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear!" That's how Habakkuk begins, in the King James. Not with a message for the people, but with the prophet arguing upward.

He sees violence and strife, the law gone slack, the wicked hemming in the righteous, and he asks why God lets him watch it. The answer troubles him more, so he asks again. Then he does something stubborn.
He climbs up to wait: "I will stand upon my watch, and set me upon the tower." He's not coming down until he hears back.

teach.h: WRITE IT PLAIN, TO READ ON THE RUN.
teach.b: The answer starts with instructions about handwriting. "Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it." Big letters, so even someone running past can read them.

teach.h: THOUGH IT TARRY, WAIT FOR IT.
teach.b: Then a warning about time: "though it tarry, wait for it."

teach.h: THE JUST SHALL LIVE BY HIS FAITH.
teach.b: Then the line: "the just shall live by his faith." The Hebrew word under faith is emunah. In English, faith can sound like a belief you hold in your head.

Emunah leans toward something you do with your whole life: steadiness, firmness, keeping faith. The same word turns up in Exodus, when Moses holds up his arms through a long battle and Aaron and Hur prop them up.
The King James says his hands were steady until the going down of the sun. Steady: that's emunah. And notice the small word his.
Some readers hear the righteous person's own steadiness. Others hear God's faithfulness, the thing the righteous lean on while they wait. The Hebrew can carry both.
Now the Talmud. In tractate Makkot, Rabbi Simlai teaches that Moses was given six hundred thirteen commandments, and later voices gathered them into fewer and fewer lines.

teach.h: ALL OF IT, SET ON ONE LINE.
teach.b: David set them on eleven, Isaiah on six, Micah on three, Isaiah again on two. For the last step the rabbis weigh Amos, then settle on this: Habakkuk came and set them all on one. The righteous shall live by his faith.
Not a rule about food or Shabbat, but the ground every rule stands on, written large enough to read on the run.

how: Jews read Habakkuk among the Twelve, and the Talmud's tractate Makkot names Habakkuk 2:4 as the single line on which the commandments stand.

games.q: you're Habakkuk. you've cried out, and the first answer troubled you more. what do you do?
o: climb the tower and wait to hear back.
games.why: "I will stand upon my watch, and set me upon the tower." the answer comes: write the vision plain, and though it tarry, wait for it.

practice: Bring to mind something you're waiting on, an answer, a result, a door to open, and like Habakkuk on the tower, choose to stand where you are rather than run.
Pick one steady thing you can trust, a person who has kept their word, a habit that holds you, or, if you pray, God's faithfulness, and let his words ride the breath: though it tarry, wait for it.

wordCard.voice: Habakkuk. The prophet who argued, climbed the tower to wait, and heard the one line that holds up the rest. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: steadiness, faithfulness; the word in "the just shall live by his faith."

carryVoice: Your line: live by faithfulness. Steady, until the going down of the sun. That's day eight hundred twenty-nine.
